title: Routines for Attention
author: Jody Chan
summary: Jody Chan argues that attention is a prerequisite for learning and that teachers need explicit, practised routines to secure it rather than treating it as something students simply provide. Drawing on Tom Sherrington's and Peps McCrea's framing of attention as 'the gatekeeper of learning,' she lays out concrete routines for two high-leverage moments: the start of an explanation and sustaining attention during it. She recommends consistent countdown scripts, standing in the same spot each time as a visual cue, and exaggerated checking for 100% compliance before beginning to speak, plus practices like cold-calling and mini-whiteboard checks to keep attention alive mid-explanation. Chan is explicit that building these routines takes time and repeated 'practice perfect' repetition, but argues the investment pays off because ignoring non-compliance embeds bad habits just as surely as enforcing routines embeds good ones.
points: Chan frames attention as the necessary first step in any learning sequence, citing McCrea's description of it as 'the gatekeeper of learning' -- essential before information can be used, remembered, retrieved, or applied.
She recommends a consistent countdown script and a fixed physical position at the start of explanations, arguing that habit-forming routines reduce the time cost of securing full attention over time.
She warns that ignoring partial non-compliance unconsciously embeds the behaviour: 'the more frequently the teacher ignores this non-compliance the more this behaviour is unconsciously embedded.'

During explanations, she recommends restating expectations, scanning for compliance, and using low-stakes questioning (mini whiteboards, cold calling at least three students on the same question) to check for listening rather than deep understanding.
quotes: Attention seems to be in the pedagogical spotlight recently. Of course, since teachers have taught getting students to concentrate on what they want them to concentrate on has been something they’ve yearned for.
Peps McCrea says 'attention is the gatekeeper of learning' and is 'essential for information to be used, remembered, retrieved, applied and retained'.
The more frequently the teacher ignores this non-compliance the more this behaviour is unconsciously embedded.

Whilst this can be true initially the more students practice the routine with no opt out the more embedded the routine becomes for all and the faster the process becomes reinforced. It is important to make sure pupils ‘practice perfect.

When you become really tuned into attention you will be able to ‘read your class,’ reading their subtle signs and signals if they have lost attention even when they are still looking at you, enabling you to notice a glazed or far-away look.
